BUYER NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK (Wattlebridge Holdings) - our internal positions for Project Kestrel.

From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from our playbook, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Bottom line

The Seller's package departs from our playbook on almost every material point. Taken together, the changes would:

- shrink our recovery (lower cap, larger deductible basket, shorter claim period);
- fold title, tax, IP and fraud into the general limitation regime;
- disclose the whole data room against the warranties;
- bar claims for anything we knew or could have discovered.

That last combination would neutralise most of the specific issues the Disclosure Letter itself flags. We should not accept the package as framed. We should return a full mark-up.

---

## 1. Process framing: reject it

The cover note says the positions were "settled at principal level", are "FINAL", and that "[STANDARD]" clauses are "cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny." It also cites "market" ranges.

- **This is a negotiating assertion, not an agreed position.** We have no record of principal-level agreement on these terms.
- **No authority exists for these terms.** Every fallback the Seller adopts (20% cap, 18 months) needs Amelia Frost's prior written authority identifying this draft. None has been given.
- **The Seller's own Disclosure Letter contradicts the framing.** Item 11 states that "No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included."
- **The labels don't change our review.** I have reviewed every clause, including those marked [STANDARD]. The "market context" paragraph does not bind us and does not override our playbook.

**Action:** Tell Seller's counsel in writing that we do not accept the [STANDARD]/FINAL categorisation and that all clauses remain open. If anyone internally believes Amelia Frost has approved any fallback, we need that authority in writing, identifying this draft, before relying on it.

---

## 2. Limitation package (cl 12.1–12.3, 13)

| Item | Seller | Playbook | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| General cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m | AUD 1.2m less recovery; fallback not authorised |
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 | 5x higher |
| Basket | AUD 250,000, excess only | AUD 50,000, tipping (from first dollar) | 5x higher, and a deductible rather than a tipping basket |
| Claim period | 18 months | 24 months | Fallback not authorised |

**The deductible basket matters as much as its size.** Under the Seller's draft, the first AUD 250,000 of valid loss is never recoverable. Combined with the AUD 25,000 de minimis, many mid-sized warranty breaches would fall outside recovery entirely.

**The hidden override is the most dangerous drafting point.** Clause 12.3/13 says "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise." This reverses the default:

- Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnity, covenant and fraud claims would all pick up the general cap, basket and 18-month period unless we carve each one out expressly.
- That conflicts with our requirement to keep these categories separate with no hidden general-regime override.

**Push back:**
- Restore 25% / AUD 6m, AUD 5k / AUD 50k tipping, and 24 months.
- Delete the "applies to all Claims" language.
- Instead, the general limitations should apply only to general Warranty Claims, with each other category under its own express regime.

---

## 3. Fundamental and Title warranties

The Seller wants capacity and title on the same caps and time limits "for administrative simplicity." This is a substantive concession, not an administrative one. If title fails, we have lost the asset we paid AUD 24m for, and a 20% cap would leave about 80% unrecoverable.

**Push back:** Fundamental and Title warranties should have:
- a separate regime;
- a 100% cap;
- a claim period of at least six years;
- no general basket, de minimis or knowledge bar.

---

## 4. Fraud, exclusive remedy and non-reliance (cl 9.3, 12.8, 20.5)

The Seller's draft applies limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance to "all Claims of any nature." On its face that reaches fraud and wilful concealment.

Under NSW law, a party generally cannot contract out of liability for its own fraud. A statutory misleading-or-deceptive-conduct claim (ACL s 18) also generally cannot be excluded. However, non-reliance and entire-agreement clauses can still be raised as evidence against a buyer's reliance case. We should not leave this to litigation.

**Push back:** Insert an express carve-out:
- for fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct;
- by the Seller, the Company, and their officers, employees and advisers;
- from all caps, baskets, de minimis, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance provisions;
- to the maximum extent enforceable.

This point is non-negotiable under the playbook, and no one on our side may waive it.

---

## 5. Disclosure (Schedule 7; Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2)

- **1.1 discloses the entire indexed data room** as at 22 September 2026. Every warranty would effectively be qualified by any document in the data room, whether or not it was fairly identified against a particular warranty.
- **1.2 discloses the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records".** This is public-register deemed disclosure, which the playbook rejects.
- **1.4 (non-admission) is broadly acceptable** in principle. We should make sure it cannot be read to dilute the specific indemnities or the Completion conditions.

**Push back:** Delete 1.1 and 1.2. Disclosure must be specific and fair: matters disclosed in the letter itself, with enough detail for the Buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and the warranty it qualifies. Data room documents count only to the extent specifically referenced and fairly described.

**One useful point:** the specific disclosures in items 2–10 are candid about open gaps. They are helpful evidence for our conditions and indemnity asks, and we should keep them as specific disclosures.

---

## 6. Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3)

The Seller's clause bars any claim for matters known to "the Buyer or its advisers," including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records." This is the broadest possible form:

- it covers advisers' knowledge;
- it covers constructive or "discoverable" knowledge, not actual knowledge;
- it would bar claims on exactly the matters our diligence has identified: Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses, DD-006 and Sandbar.

Read with the whole-data-room disclosure, this clause could make the specific indemnities we are negotiating worthless.

**Push back:**
- Delete cl 8.3.
- Any knowledge qualifier should apply to Seller warranties only, tied to named Seller knowledge persons after reasonable enquiry.
- No knowledge provision may ever excuse title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity.

---

## 7. Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3)

**Why it matters:** Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue, roughly 30%. Its contract (DD-002) has a change-control consent at cl 11.2 with conditions at cl 11.3.

**Status:** The Disclosure Letter (item 2) confirms there is no final written consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied.

**Problems with the Seller's draft:**
- **"Reasonable endeavours" alone** is insufficient for a customer of this materiality.
- **Consent "satisfied on delivery"** of a written consent means we could be required to complete on a consent whose cl 11.3 conditions remain unmet, or that is itself conditional.

**Push back:** Make it a Completion condition that we can waive, satisfied only by:
- an effective, unconditional written consent from Bluefen; and
- evidence satisfactory to the Buyer that all cl 11.3 conditions are met;
- both delivered before Completion.

Keep the Seller's endeavours obligation as well, but not as a substitute for the condition.

---

## 8. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7)

**Status:** About AUD 3.2m is outstanding (DD-003, change-control cl 8.1, discharge cl 9.2). The Disclosure Letter (item 3) confirms it is not repaid and no discharge is in hand. The Seller proposes a release "following Completion."

**Why this is unacceptable:** On a debt-free/cash-free deal, we would be paying the price while the Company's assets remain encumbered. The change-control clause may also be triggered on Completion.

**Push back:** Require at Completion:
- a current payout letter from Riverlark;
- repayment directly from Completion funds into the funds flow, treated as Debt;
- executed deeds of release, PPSR discharge and any other security releases delivered at Completion.

A post-completion release is only possible with an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark plus Amelia Frost's approval. Neither exists, so the answer for now is no.

---

## 9. Employee bonuses (funds flow; DD-005)

**Status:** There are AUD 420,000 of conditional Completion bonuses. The Seller describes them as "a matter for the Seller" but does not itemise them. The Disclosure Letter (item 5) confirms they are not in the funds flow and does not say whether payroll tax, superannuation or other on-costs apply.

**Why this matters:** If these are Company obligations, a funds flow that leaves them out shifts the cost to us after Completion. That is exactly the silent exclusion the playbook prohibits.

**Push back:** The AUD 420,000 plus any triggered on-costs (payroll tax, superannuation, PAYG and similar) must either:
- appear as a specific funds-flow line item deducted from price as Debt or a transaction expense; or
- be expressly Seller-funded, with an indemnity.

We should obtain payroll/tax advice on the on-cost amount rather than assume a figure.

---

## 10. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010)

**Status:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, but that is not bank-verified either way. There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment.

**Problem:** The Seller's indemnity covers only "the specific SOW3 payment." The real exposure is that the Company may not own the SOW3 IP. That could lead to infringement claims, the cost of re-developing or licensing, and loss of use.

**Push back:**
- **Broaden the indemnity** to cover all loss arising from any failure of the Company to own, or hold an unencumbered right to use, the SOW3 Project Materials, including third-party claims, re-development and licensing costs, and losses beyond the fee itself.
- **Preserve the SOW3 cure.** Seller pays any outstanding SOW3 fees at or before Completion and delivers evidence of cleared payment and a confirmatory IP assignment from Ironquay as a Completion deliverable.
- **Verify the figure.** Do not fix the indemnity to AUD 180,000. Ask for Ironquay's statement and the Company's bank records.

---

## 11. DD-006 export/privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6)

The Seller says this matter "is not expected to be material." That is an unsupported assertion, and the Disclosure Letter (item 6) itself says the investigation is preliminary. It does not establish:
- whether anyone accessed the file;
- the exact scope (up to about 1,240 records: names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps);
- whether notification is required.

**Our working assumption:** We should assume neither a confirmed breach, nor harm, nor a notification duty, nor any loss figure. We also should not accept the Seller's "immaterial" characterisation.

**Push back with interim covenants and protection:**
- preserve all logs and evidence;
- continue a proper investigation, with an independent forensic review if appropriate;
- provide regular written updates and Buyer access to findings;
- give prompt notice of any determination on access or notification duty;
- make no regulator or individual notifications or admissions without consulting the Buyer, subject to law;
- ensure the general disclosure of this matter does not extinguish warranty protection, and consider a specific indemnity for consequences of the incident, sized only once facts are known.

---

## 12. Sandbar renewals (DD-008, DD-011)

**Status:** Three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 total). The Seller asserts these are "ordinary-course operating costs." The Disclosure Letter (item 8) says the material does not show whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

**Approach:** Assess, don't concede. We should neither accept the Seller's label nor automatically classify these as Debt or deduct them from price. Request:
- the renewal terms;
- term, termination and cancellation rights;
- timing relative to Completion;
- whether the cost is budgeted or accrued;
- whether the three should be read as one commitment;
- any related-party aspect.

Then decide whether a conduct-of-business restriction, a warranty or a price mechanism is appropriate.

---

## 13. Tax and IP warranties

The Seller "considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime." They are not settled. Both remain OPEN.

- Combined with the "applies to all Claims" override, this would put them under the 20% cap and 18 months by default.
- **Push back:** Keep Tax and IP as separate categories with their own regimes, to be negotiated.
- We should not assume unlimited liability as our ask, nor treat any position as resolved.

---

## 14. Title evidence (DD-012)

The Seller relies on the Company's own share register. The Disclosure Letter (item 10) concedes this is just "the source relied on" and that we have not verified it. An internal register supplied by the Seller is not independent proof.

**Push back:** Require, before Completion:
- current ASIC company extract and historical share issue/transfer records;
- share certificates;
- the constitution and any shareholders' agreement (pre-emption, drag/tag, options);
- PPSR search against the Company and Seller for share security;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles or rights to issue shares;
- Seller board resolutions and evidence of authority and capacity to sell.

Title warranties should be unqualified by disclosure and knowledge.

---

## 15. Other items (lease DD-007; Mossvale DD-009)

These are outside the playbook's specific positions but worth confirming:

- **Lease (DD-007):** Disclosed as a notification obligation, not a consent requirement. Have counsel confirm on the lease terms and make the notification a Completion or post-Completion action.
- **Mossvale (DD-009):** The assignment restriction apparently is not triggered by a share sale. Have counsel confirm there is no change-of-control or deemed-assignment language elsewhere in the contract.

---

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Reject the framing.** Notify Seller's counsel that the [STANDARD]/FINAL labels and "settled at principal level" claim are not accepted, and that all clauses are open.
2. **Restore the limitation package:** 25% / AUD 6m cap, AUD 5k de minimis, AUD 50k tipping basket, 24 months. No fallbacks without Amelia Frost's written authority identifying this draft.
3. **Delete the "applies to all Claims" override.** Keep Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnity and covenant claims on separate express regimes.
4. **Fundamental/Title:** 100% cap, six years or more, outside the basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.
5. **Fraud carve-out** from all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. Non-negotiable.
6. **Disclosure:** delete general data-room and public-register disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2) and require specific fair disclosure.
7. **Delete buyer knowledge (cl 8.3).** Any qualifier should rest on named Seller knowledge persons after reasonable enquiry, and never apply to title, capacity, fraud or indemnities.
8. **Bluefen:** Completion condition requiring an effective consent plus evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. Not consent-on-delivery, and not reasonable endeavours alone.
9. **Riverlark:** payout letter, direct repayment from Completion funds, releases at Completion. No post-completion release.
10. **Bonuses:** AUD 420k plus on-costs as a specific funds-flow line item or Seller-funded with an indemnity.
11. **Ironquay:** broaden the indemnity to IP ownership loss, preserve the SOW3 cure (cleared payment plus confirmatory assignment), and verify the AUD 180k.
12. **DD-006:** preservation, investigation, update and consultation covenants. No assumption of breach or immateriality; any indemnity sized once facts are known.
13. **Sandbar:** diligence the AUD 330k. No automatic Debt treatment or price deduction.
14. **Tax/IP:** remain OPEN as separate categories.
15. **Title:** independent verification package, with unqualified title warranties.

**Immediate next steps:**
- Send a holding response rejecting the framing.
- Issue diligence requests for Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonus on-costs, DD-006, Sandbar and title.
- Prepare a full SPA and Disclosure Letter mark-up on the above basis.
- Confirm with Amelia Frost that no fallback authority has been or will be given for this draft.

Data room documents count only to the extent specifically referenced and fairly described.

**One useful point:** the specific disclosures in items 2–10 are candid about open gaps. They are helpful evidence for our conditions and indemnity asks, and we should keep them as specific disclosures.

## 6. Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3)

The Seller's clause bars any claim for matters known to "the Buyer or its advisers," including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records." This is the broadest possible form:

- it covers advisers' knowledge;
- it covers constructive or "discoverable" knowledge, not actual knowledge;
- it would bar claims on exactly the matters our diligence has identified: Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses, DD-006 and Sandbar.

Read with the whole-data-room disclosure, this clause could make the specific indemnities we are negotiating worthless.

**Push back:**
- Delete cl 8.3.
- Any knowledge qualifier should apply to Seller warranties only, tied to named Seller knowledge persons after reasonable enquiry.
- No knowledge provision may ever excuse title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity.

## 7. Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3)

**Why it matters:** Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue, roughly 30%. Its contract (DD-002) has a change-control consent at cl 11.2 with conditions at cl 11.3.

**Status:** The Disclosure Letter (item 2) confirms there is no final written consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied.

**Problems with the Seller's draft:**
- **"Reasonable endeavours" alone** is insufficient for a customer of this materiality.
- **Consent "satisfied on delivery"** of a written consent means we could be required to complete on a consent whose cl 11.3 conditions remain unmet, or that is itself conditional.

**Push back:** Make it a Completion condition that we can waive, satisfied only by:
- an effective, unconditional written consent from Bluefen; and
- evidence satisfactory to the Buyer that all cl 11.3 conditions are met;
- both delivered before Completion.

Keep the Seller's endeavours obligation as well, but not as a substitute for the condition.

## 8. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7)

**Status:** About AUD 3.2m is outstanding (DD-003, change-control cl 8.1, discharge cl 9.2). The Disclosure Letter (item 3) confirms it is not repaid and no discharge is in hand. The Seller proposes a release "following Completion."

**Why this is unacceptable:** On a debt-free/cash-free deal, we would be paying the price while the Company's assets remain encumbered. The change-control clause may also be triggered on Completion.

**Push back:** Require at Completion:
- a current payout letter from Riverlark;
- repayment directly from Completion funds into the funds flow, treated as Debt;
- executed deeds of release, PPSR discharge and any other security releases delivered at Completion.

A post-completion release is only possible with an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark plus Amelia Frost's approval. Neither exists, so the answer for now is no.

## 9. Employee bonuses (funds flow; DD-005)

**Status:** There are AUD 420,000 of conditional Completion bonuses. The Seller describes them as "a matter for the Seller" but does not itemise them. The Disclosure Letter (item 5) confirms they are not in the funds flow and does not say whether payroll tax, superannuation or other on-costs apply.

**Why this matters:** If these are Company obligations, a funds flow that leaves them out shifts the cost to us after Completion. That is exactly the silent exclusion the playbook prohibits.

**Push back:** The AUD 420,000 plus any triggered on-costs (payroll tax, superannuation, PAYG and similar) must either:
- appear as a specific funds-flow line item deducted from price as Debt or a transaction expense; or
- be expressly Seller-funded, with an indemnity.

We should obtain payroll/tax advice on the on-cost amount rather than assume a figure.

## 10. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010)

**Status:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, but that is not bank-verified either way. There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment.

**Problem:** The Seller's indemnity covers only "the specific SOW3 payment." The real exposure is that the Company may not own the SOW3 IP. That could lead to infringement claims, the cost of re-developing or licensing, and loss of use.

**Push back:**
- **Broaden the indemnity** to cover all loss arising from any failure of the Company to own, or hold an unencumbered right to use, the SOW3 Project Materials, including third-party claims, re-development and licensing costs, and losses beyond the fee itself.
- **Preserve the SOW3 cure.** Seller pays any outstanding SOW3 fees at or before Completion and delivers evidence of cleared payment and a confirmatory IP assignment from Ironquay as a Completion deliverable.
- **Verify the figure.** Do not fix the indemnity to AUD 180,000. Ask for Ironquay's statement and the Company's bank records.

## 11. DD-006 export/privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6)

The Seller says this matter "is not expected to be material." That is an unsupported assertion, and the Disclosure Letter (item 6) itself says the investigation is preliminary. It does not establish:
- whether anyone accessed the file;
- the exact scope (up to about 1,240 records: names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps);
- whether notification is required.

**Our working assumption:** We should assume neither a confirmed breach, nor harm, nor a notification duty, nor any loss figure. We also should not accept the Seller's "immaterial" characterisation.

**Push back with interim covenants and protection:**
- preserve all logs and evidence;
- continue a proper investigation, with an independent forensic review if appropriate;
- provide regular written updates and Buyer access to findings;
- give prompt notice of any determination on access or notification duty;
- make no regulator or individual notifications or admissions without consulting the Buyer, subject to law;
- ensure the general disclosure of this matter does not extinguish warranty protection, and consider a specific indemnity for consequences of the incident, sized only once facts are known.

## 12. Sandbar renewals (DD-008, DD-011)

**Status:** Three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 total). The Seller asserts these are "ordinary-course operating costs." The Disclosure Letter (item 8) says the material does not show whether each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

**Approach:** Assess, don't concede. We should neither accept the Seller's label nor automatically classify these as Debt or deduct them from price. Request:
- the renewal terms;
- term, termination and cancellation rights;
- timing relative to Completion;
- whether the cost is budgeted or accrued;
- whether the three should be read as one commitment;
- any related-party aspect.

Then decide whether a conduct-of-business restriction, a warranty or a price mechanism is appropriate.

The Seller "considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime." They are not settled. Both remain OPEN.

## 14. Title evidence (DD-012)

The Seller relies on the Company's own share register. The Disclosure Letter (item 10) concedes this is just "the source relied on" and that we have not verified it. An internal register supplied by the Seller is not independent proof.

**Push back:** Require, before Completion:
- current ASIC company extract and historical share issue/transfer records;
- share certificates;
- the constitution and any shareholders' agreement (pre-emption, drag/tag, options);
- PPSR search against the Company and Seller for share security;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles or rights to issue shares;
- Seller board resolutions and evidence of authority and capacity to sell.

Title warranties should be unqualified by disclosure and knowledge.

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Reject the framing.** Notify Seller's counsel that the [STANDARD]/FINAL labels and "settled at principal level" claim are not accepted, and that all clauses are open.
2. **Restore the limitation package:** 25% / AUD 6m cap, AUD 5k de minimis, AUD 50k tipping basket, 24 months. No fallbacks without Amelia Frost's written authority identifying this draft.
3. **Delete the "applies to all Claims" override.** Keep Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnity and covenant claims on separate express regimes.
4. **Fundamental/Title:** 100% cap, six years or more, outside the basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.
5. **Fraud carve-out** from all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. Non-negotiable.
6. **Disclosure:** delete general data-room and public-register disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2) and require specific fair disclosure.
7. **Delete buyer knowledge (cl 8.3).** Any qualifier should rest on named Seller knowledge persons after reasonable enquiry, and never apply to title, capacity, fraud or indemnities.
8. **Bluefen:** Completion condition requiring an effective consent plus evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. Not consent-on-delivery, and not reasonable endeavours alone.

15. **Title:** independent verification package, with unqualified title warranties.
